#9783. A trailing slash on our site is a 308, a capital letter is a 404, and /. is the homepage answering 200

The URL a reader asks for is not always the URL you published. It arrives with a UTM parameter stapled on, or with a trailing slash from a CMS, or capitalised because somebody typed it off a slide, or with a doubled slash because two bits of string concatenation both added one.

Notifio's site is 38 pages. I have audited what those 38 URLs are before. This time I asked for each of them three different wrong ways, recorded the status code, the redirect target, the , the canonical and every robots meta, and then went after the odd shapes by hand.</p> <p>For each of the 38 paths: add a trailing slash, upper-case the whole path, add ?utm_source=devto.</p> <p>The 37s are 38 minus the homepage, where all three variants are the same request. Consistent, which is the boring answer I was hoping for. Two parts of it are worth saying out loud though.</p> <p>The path is case sensitive and the query string is not part of the identity. /HELP is not a page. /help?utm_source=devto is /help, and it says so: all 38 query variants emit a canonical pointing at the clean URL, with zero exceptions. Those two behaviours together mean the number of distinct URLs that serve our 38 pages is infinite, and the only thing stopping that from being 38 duplicate-content problems is one <link rel="canonical"> per page.</p> <p>The redirect is cheap and the 404 is not free. A 308 is 15 bytes of body. Our 404 is 13,627 bytes, which is a full page, and the route census that first found it explains why it reads the way it does.</p> <p>/help// is a two-hop redirect. It goes to /help/, which is itself a redirect to /help. A doubled trailing slash costs a reader two round trips, and a crawler two hops of its link-equity budget, where the single slash costs one.</p> <p>/HELP/ redirects into a 404. The slash normalisation runs before anything knows whether the path exists, so an upper-cased URL with a trailing slash gets a 308 to an upper-cased URL without one, and then a 404. Two requests to be told no. There is nothing wrong with this, and it is a good reminder that redirect rules do not know about your routes.</p> <p>/%68elp is /help. Percent-encoding is decoded before routing, so an encoded lower-case h works and the page comes back with the correct canonical. /%48ELP does not work, because it decodes to /HELP, and we are back to case sensitivity. Encoding is transparent, case is not.</p> <p>/. answers 200 with the homepage. Title, canonical, full 93,725 bytes of it:</p> <p>And its robots meta is index, follow, so that URL is indexable. The canonical is the only thing keeping it from being a second copy of our homepage in a search index. I did not write a rule that allows /. and I cannot find a reason to want one, but the mitigation was already in place before I knew the problem existed, which is the best advertisement for self-referencing canonicals I have.</p> <p>/success is the one page with no canonical at all. It is the page Stripe sends people to after paying, it is not in the sitemap, and it carries noindex, nofollow, which is right. It is also the page our robots.txt tries to protect with a rule that does not match it:</p> <p>Disallow: /success/ is a literal prefix, and the page is at /success with no slash. That one I had already found and written about, and seeing it again from the other end, by asking the URL instead of reading the rule, is a good argument for measuring from outside.</p> <p>The 307 on /maintenance is ours: one boolean in the repository decides whether that route renders or sends you home, and with the switch off it sends you home. It is the only 307 in this whole sweep, because it is the only redirect we wrote ourselves rather than inherited.</p> <p>Unknown slugs inside our four dynamic route spaces answer differently from unknown paths:</p> <p>Four route spaces, four 404s within six bytes of each other, all of them wearing the homepage's title, and a completely different 404 for everything else. Both flavours emit two robots metas, noindex and then index, follow, which is the contradiction my earlier route census found and which this sweep now confirms from the wire. The cause is the same in both: there is no not-found.tsx in the app, so the layout's metadata and the framework's default 404 are both rendering.</p> <p>Fixing: the missing not-found.tsx. Several of the measurements above are symptoms of that one gap, and a reader who mistypes a URL currently gets a page whose title says it is the homepage.</p> <p>Fixing: the homepage's own canonical. Our sitemap publishes https://notifio.app/ and the page itself emits https://notifio.app. Both resolve, Google treats them as the same URL, and there is still no good reason for a site's two most authoritative statements about its own front door to disagree by one character.</p> <p>Not fixing: case sensitivity. A case-insensitive router means every page has 2^n names, and a 404 is a clearer answer than a redirect from a URL nobody published.</p> <p>Not fixing: /. or the percent-encoded variants. The canonical already handles them, and a rewrite rule for every string that normalises to a real path is a bigger surface than the problem.</p> <p>If you want the version of this you can run in a minute, it is one line per shape:</p> <p>The pages I used are all live: /help, /alerts/kamernet, /compare/rentbird and /guides/rental-scams-netherlands. Notifio is at notifio.app and the app it sells is on the download page.</p> <p>DEV Community — A space to discuss and keep up software development and manage your software career</p> <p>Built on Forem — the open source software that powers DEV and other inclusive communities.</p> <p>Made with love and Ruby on Rails. DEV Community © 2016 - 2026.</p> <p>We're a place where coders share, stay up-to-date and grow their careers.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://dev.to/daniel_pertu/a-trailing-slash-on-our-site-is-a-308-a-capital-letter-is-a-404-and-is-the-homepage-answering-1n3b" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9782"> <h2>#9782. 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://huggingface.co/blog/assets/moe-expert-streaming/thumbnail.png" alt="180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.</p> <p>I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.</p> <p>Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.</p> <p>I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.</p> <p>My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.</p> <p>When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.</p> <p>Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!</p> <p>It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.</p> <p>That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.</p> <p>Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?</p> <p>llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.</p> <p>vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.</p> <p>Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.</p> <p>I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:</p> <p>Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.</p> <p>If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.</p> <p>Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.</p> <p>All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.</p> <p>I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.</p> <p>First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.</p> <p>The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.</p> <p>I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:</p> <p>Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:</p> <p>That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.</p> <p>Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.</p> <p>The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.</p> <p>Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:</p> <p>The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.</p> <p>The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.</p> <p>Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:</p> <p>Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.</p> <p>I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.</p> <p>Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:</p> <p>Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:</p> <p>These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:</p> <p>That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.</p> <p>Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.</p> <p>It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.</p> <p>Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.</p> <p>Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.</p> <p>The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.</p> <p>Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.</p> <p>Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.</p> <p>Generate text with Qwen3.8 using streamed experts</p> <p>Generate text with Qwen3.8 using streamed experts</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://huggingface.co/blog/moe-expert-streaming" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9781"> <h2>#9781. Removing a green screen in code: what I learned open-sourcing a video matting pipeline</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=1200,height=627,fit=cover,gravity=auto,format=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fqjbmshaut98h8a38at35.png" alt="Removing a green screen in code: what I learned open-sourcing a video matting pipeline" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>This pipeline started as the Standard pipeline behind Zapmatte, the hosted green screen remover I run: upload a clip on the website, get a transparent video back. The hosted version made the workflow a form instead of a timeline — but every step inside it was still code, and code can be shared. So I took that pipeline, cleaned it up, and open-sourced it. This post is the tutorial I wish I had at the start: what the pipeline does, in what order, and how to run it.</p> <p>A plain chroma key works until it doesn't. The screen is never evenly lit, shadows fall on it, and the moment your subject has flyaway hair, the key either eats the hair or leaves a green halo. An AI matting model has the opposite problem: it is good at people and soft edges, but it does not know your props exist, and it can wobble from frame to frame.</p> <p>The pipeline I ended up with uses both, each where it is strong:</p> <p>You need Python 3.10+ and ffmpeg (with libvpx and prores_ks) on your PATH.</p> <p>The RVM weights download from GitHub on the first run, via torch.hub. After that:</p> <p>This took me longer to learn than the keying itself:</p> <p>Resolution (up to 4K) and audio are kept. On a T4 GPU it runs about 41 fps at 720p, 19 fps at 1080p and 5.5 fps at 4K. It also runs on CPU, slowly — fine for a short clip, painful for a long one.</p> <p>The repo is GPL-3.0, because it builds on Robust Video Matting (also GPL-3.0 — please cite their paper if you use this in research). If you'd rather not install anything, the same pipeline runs on the Zapmatte website — upload a clip, download the result, first 10 seconds free.</p> <p>If you try it on your own footage and hit an edge case I haven't covered, open an issue — real-world clips are how this thing gets better.</p> <p>DEV Community — A space to discuss and keep up software development and manage your software career</p> <p>Built on Forem — the open source software that powers DEV and other inclusive communities.</p> <p>Made with love and Ruby on Rails. DEV Community © 2016 - 2026.</p> <p>We're a place where coders share, stay up-to-date and grow their careers.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://dev.to/gabriellaandrews/removing-a-green-screen-in-code-what-i-learned-open-sourcing-a-video-matting-pipeline-35bl" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9780"> <h2>#9780. Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/64e8143f6de557454220921e/yf6E9vJHIkGHG_toGSasb.gif" alt="Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.</p> <p>Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.</p> <p>The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.</p> <p>IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.</p> <p>Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.</p> <p>Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them</p> <p>Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.</p> <p>The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.</p> <p>See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:</p> <p>Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.</p> <p>A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.</p> <p>Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.</p> <p>Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.</p> <p>Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.</p> <p>This approach can help teams in four ways:</p> <p>-Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.</p> <p>-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.</p> <p>-Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.</p> <p>-Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.</p> <p>Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent</p> <p>The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.</p> <p>An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.</p> <p>To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.</p> <p>When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.</p> <p>The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.</p> <p>Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.</p> <p>A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.</p> <p>AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.</p> <p>When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.</p> <p>Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.</p> <p>A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.</p> <p>With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.</p> <p>When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.</p> <p>Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.</p> <p>Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.</p> <p>A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.</p> <p>The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.</p> <p>Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.</p> <p>An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.</p> <p>On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.</p> <p>If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.</p> <p>Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.</p> <p>A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.</p> <p>TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.</p> <p>This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.</p> <p>Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.</p> <p>The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:</p> <p>Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.</p> <p>Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.</p> <p>Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.</p> <p>Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.</p> <p>In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.</p> <p>Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.</p> <p>Code and notebooks: github.com/ibm-granite/granite-tsfm</p> <p>Real-Time Intelligence with IBM Time Series Models on Confluent</p> <p>Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models</p> <p>IBM releases SOTA Granite Time Series PatchTST-FM-r2 model with commercial-friendly license</p> <p>New in Confluent Intelligence and AI Tools: Making Agents Native to the Stream, Expanded Model Support, New Agent Skills, and Confluent Assistant</p> <p>What's New in Q4'26 Confluent Data Streaming Platform</p> <p>What's New for Confluent Platform for Apache Flink, November 2026</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://huggingface.co/blog/ibm-research/time-series-powered-streamhouse" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9779"> <h2>#9779. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p><h2 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> </span></h2><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEjbDTd3znkB-FhGnQL-V8kUsAXIlJaksqIPyM9X0IoE1Yq0zomkIHOZNIXFw83utgtxHLJaBoC_cQnAgR8w-xLkzmkSs5JbWBrCyFzNva6va-yu_T1v224t7i-8JZ6hybYjhw2oCHnqrmeN07VxMpMQ2GuXb7KHbn8ocHU20WyiD_CK3BQXUIxGSCQS2A=s1920" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="Sellfy" border="0" height="360" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEjbDTd3znkB-FhGnQL-V8kUsAXIlJaksqIPyM9X0IoE1Yq0zomkIHOZNIXFw83utgtxHLJaBoC_cQnAgR8w-xLkzmkSs5JbWBrCyFzNva6va-yu_T1v224t7i-8JZ6hybYjhw2oCHnqrmeN07VxMpMQ2GuXb7KHbn8ocHU20WyiD_CK3BQXUIxGSCQS2A=w640-h360" title="Sellfy" width="640" /></a></span></div><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><br /></span><p></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.</span></p><h2 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">What is Sellfy?</span></h2><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><a href="https://get.sellfy.com/crunchhype" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Sellfy </a>is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Features</span></h3><p style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa; font-weight: normal;">Sellfy includes:</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Online Store</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><a href="https://get.sellfy.com/crunchhype" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Sellfy </a>is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><a href="https://get.sellfy.com/crunchhype" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Sellfy </a>gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Product hosting</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><a href="https://get.sellfy.com/crunchhype" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Sellfy </a>allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Embed options</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Payments and security</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.</span></p> <br /> <div id="atContainer-8a426783aef805554f3d96c19f8beeb7"></div> <h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Marketing and analytics tools</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">The Sellfy platform includes marketing and analytics tools to help you manage your online store. You can send email product updates and collect newsletter subscribers through the platform. With Sellfy, you can also offer discount codes and product upsells, as well as create and track Facebook and Twitter ads for your store. The software's analytics dashboard will help you track your best-performing products, generated revenue, traffic channels, top locations, and overall store performance.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Integrations</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: How to get a daily list of new UK companies from Companies House with Python</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=1200,height=627,fit=cover,gravity=auto,format=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fc4v7dcvub00wn9dr0n33.png" alt="How to get a daily list of new UK companies from Companies House with Python" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Disclosure: I built the Apify actor used in the second half of this post. It is a paid tool (pay per company). The first half is free and uses only the public Companies House register.</p> <p>Every weekday, between 2,000 and 3,500 new companies are incorporated in the UK. A new company needs an accountant, a bank account, insurance, payroll, a website, an office and suppliers, and it usually chooses them in its first few weeks. If you sell any of those, the Companies House register is one of the best lead sources there is: it is official, it is updated every day, and it is free to search.</p> <p>This post shows how to turn the register into a daily lead list with Python: first the free way, then a hosted version that adds filters, directors and only-new delivery.</p> <p>For every company Companies House publishes:</p> <p>SIC codes are the key to filtering. They are five-digit codes, grouped by their first two digits: 41-43 construction, 56 food and drink service, 62 software and IT, 68 real estate, 69 legal and accounting, 86 health. Code 99999 means a dormant company that does not trade.</p> <p>The Companies House website has an advanced search with an incorporation-date filter and a "Download results" button that returns a CSV of up to 5,000 companies. One day of incorporations fits in one download, so this works from Python:</p> <p>Two things to know before you build on this:</p> <p>That gives you the raw list. The usual next steps are filtering by industry and area, adding directors (one officers page per company), remembering which companies you already sent to your CRM, and running it on a schedule.</p> <p>UK New Companies is the Apify actor I built for this. It downloads each day from the register, fixes the SIC column, adds SIC descriptions and the industry section, splits out the postcode, filters, optionally adds active officers, and remembers what it already delivered.</p> <p>You need a free Apify account and your API token (Console, then Settings, then API & Integrations). Then pip install "apify-client>=3" and run this. It finds new construction companies in Greater Manchester from the last 7 days, with directors:</p> <p>The name, number, address and director below are made up:</p> <p>With includeOfficers on, each row also has officers with name, first and last name, role and appointment date. Dates of birth, nationalities and home addresses, which the register also shows, are left out on purpose: a lead list does not need them.</p> <p>For a running feed, add onlyNew and a stateKey:</p> <p>Each run delivers only companies that earlier runs with the same stateKey have not delivered. Keep a 3-day window even for a daily run: the register is updated during the day, so a company can appear a day after its incorporation date. Then save the input as a task in Apify Console and add a daily schedule, and send new rows to Google Sheets, HubSpot, Slack or a webhook with an integration, Make, Zapier or n8n.</p> <p>$3 per 1,000 companies on the free plan, with lower rates on paid Apify plans. Companies removed by your filters and companies a monitor already delivered are not billed. All companies incorporated in a full week, about 15,000, take about ten seconds and cost about $45; a filtered list such as one industry in one city is usually a few dozen companies a day, a few cents.</p> <p>Company data on the register is public, but UK GDPR and PECR still apply when you contact directors. Have a legitimate interest, say who you are, keep the message relevant to the business, and offer an easy opt-out. The register has no email addresses or phone numbers; most people use the registered office for letters or look up the company's website.</p> <p>Questions or a wrong row? Open an issue on the actor's Issues tab with the company number and your run ID. I read them daily.</p> <p>DEV Community — A space to discuss and keep up software development and manage your software career</p> <p>Built on Forem — the open source software that powers DEV and other inclusive communities.</p> <p>Made with love and Ruby on Rails. DEV Community © 2016 - 2026.</p> <p>We're a place where coders share, stay up-to-date and grow their careers.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://dev.to/mustapha11/how-to-get-a-daily-list-of-new-uk-companies-from-companies-house-with-python-1l8k" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9777"> <h2>#9777. The HackerNoon Newsletter: Fridges, Hackers, AI and La Flemme (11/21/2026)</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://hackernoon.imgix.net/images/hackernoon_newsletter_98_khkxg33ivfl242o0dktn1t1c.png" alt="The HackerNoon Newsletter: Fridges, Hackers, AI and La Flemme (11/21/2026)" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Get Hacker Noon's top homepage stories delivered to your inbox every day at noon</p> <p>Get Hacker Noon's top homepage stories delivered to your inbox every day at noon</p> <p>Get Hacker Noon's top homepage stories delivered to your inbox every day at noon</p> <p>🪐 What’s happening in tech today, November 21, 2026?</p> <p>The HackerNoon Newsletter brings the HackerNoon homepage straight to your inbox. On this day, we present you with these top quality stories. From Europe’s Democracy Is at Risk If It Cannot Control the AI It Depends On to Benchmarking AWS Amplify, Lambda, Web Functions, and ECS for Next.js, let’s dive right in.</p> <p>By @tokarevartem [ 19 Min read ] A hands-on benchmark comparing AWS Amplify, Lambda, Web Functions, and ECS for Next.js, covering latency, cold starts, scaling, and monthly costs. Read More.</p> <p>By @product [ 3 Min read ] Get interviewed and share your expertise on HackerNoon with Journalistic.tech. Explore 273 interview templates and turn your answers into a story. Read More.</p> <p>By @rscyber [ 8 Min read ] How AI lowers the barrier to attacking industrial controllers, using the Danfoss fridge hacks that hit European supermarkets. Read More.</p> <p>By @francescocapria [ 21 Min read ] Europe is easing data rules for AI while relying on models it doesn’t control. From Fable 5 to PHP2Shell, what that dependence means for Europe. Read More.</p> <p>🧑‍💻 What happened in your world this week?</p> <p>It's been said that writing can help consolidate technical knowledge, establish credibility, and contribute to emerging community standards. Feeling stuck? We got you covered ⬇️⬇️⬇️</p> <p>ANSWER THESE GREATEST INTERVIEW QUESTIONS OF ALL TIME</p> <p>We hope you enjoy this worth of free reading material. Feel free to forward this email to a nerdy friend who'll love you for it.See you on Planet Internet! With love, The HackerNoon Team ✌️</p> <p>The HackerNoon Newsletter: Creating the Intelligent Being; the AI Alien (11/20/2026)</p> <p>Get Hacker Noon's top homepage stories delivered to your inbox every day at noon</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://hackernoon.com/11-21-2026-newsletter?source=rss" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9776"> <h2>#9776. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/6a725daa5ca641a21ab61956/J6DIf4Len_31Tj-CQlQXY.png" alt="Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.</p> <p>A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.</p> <p>GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.</p> <p>Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.</p> <p>We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.</p> <p>The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.</p> <p>For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:</p> <p>Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.</p> <p>This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.</p> <p>These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.</p> <p>To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.</p> <p>We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.</p> <p>We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.</p> <p>Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.</p> <p>All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.</p> <p>No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.</p> <p>A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.</p> <p>Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.</p> <p>Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.</p> <p>CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.</p> <p>Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).</p> <p>Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.</p> <p>One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.</p> <p>Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:</p> <p>Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.</p> <p>Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.</p> <p>More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.</p> <p>In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.</p> <p>What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.</p> <p>Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.</p> <p>The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://huggingface.co/blog/Dharma-AI/predicting-fine-tuning-time" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9775"> <h2>#9775. Designing a Hint System That Does Not Spoil the Answer</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=1200,height=627,fit=cover,gravity=auto,format=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F1konkgu3q0oqafbk8a5u.png" alt="Designing a Hint System That Does Not Spoil the Answer" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>A hint system is a negotiation between two goals. The player asking for help wants to make progress. The designer wants to preserve the moment of realisation that makes the game worth playing. Most hint systems fail by picking one side.</p> <p>The system I ended up with is graded. The first hint is about the route, not the word: it tells you which move you are stuck on and what kind of change that move probably involves. The second level narrows the target position. The third gives you a letter. You have to ask for each one, and the game records that you did.</p> <p>The important design choice is that no level reveals the answer. At the deepest level you are still solving; you have simply replaced some of the search space with information. That keeps the player in the loop and prevents today's puzzle from turning into a thing you watch rather than a thing you do.</p> <p>There is a second-order benefit to grading, which is that people use hints differently. Some players take one hint almost every day and treat it as part of the ritual. Others take none for weeks and then spend all three in a single bad sitting. A single all-or-nothing hint optimises for neither.</p> <p>The layout matters more than I expected. Hints have to be visible where the player is stuck, not behind a settings menu, and they have to be cheap to dismiss. A hint the player did not want is worse than no hint at all, because it removes the sense that the board was theirs.</p> <p>One thing I would not do again: hiding the hint counter. Players who know the count is tracked behave differently than players who do not, and not in a good way. Making the count explicit made the system feel fair.</p> <p>If you are copying this, the graded approach is the part to keep. It fits naturally with unlimited practice, where the cost of a hint is only the time you spend, and it gives you a simple rule for every level above the first: never give information the player could have derived from the board.</p> <p>DEV Community — A space to discuss and keep up software development and manage your software career</p> <p>Built on Forem — the open source software that powers DEV and other inclusive communities.</p> <p>Made with love and Ruby on Rails. DEV Community © 2016 - 2026.</p> <p>We're a place where coders share, stay up-to-date and grow their careers.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://dev.to/poopleunlimited/designing-a-hint-system-that-does-not-spoil-the-answer-5de" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9774"> <h2>#9774. One Row Lied to the Whole Team</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=1200,height=627,fit=cover,gravity=auto,format=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F64fg7nlwi40nsvo5igkn.png" alt="One Row Lied to the Whole Team" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>A story about exactly-once, one restart, and the question nobody dared to ask.</p> <p>Mei posted three words in the team channel: "Verified. Ship it."</p> <p>Five minutes earlier, the order pipeline had come back from a restart. In the target table, order 8821 was a single row: PAID, 1299.00. Identical to MySQL. Primary key matched. Value matched. Even the decimals matched.</p> <p>Ravi replied: "How many rows did you check?"</p> <p>"All of them," Mei said. "Twenty-three thousand. Not one missing."</p> <p>It was the last release window before the quarter closed. The pipeline had already slipped twice. Our PM in Singapore had asked three times whether we could ship that day. Everyone exhaled.</p> <p>Ravi said nothing. Later, I found what he had written in his notebook:</p> <p>"All we proved was that it looked right."</p> <p>Six weeks later, that distinction cost us a compliance finding.</p> <p>Her checklist had seven items — row count, primary key, amount, status, timestamp, encoding, null handling. She checked every one against the source. Twenty-three thousand rows, not one missing. That is a clean, professional verification.</p> <p>The problem is that all seven questions were the same question:</p> <p>"At the moment of the query, what value does this key hold?"</p> <p>But exactly-once promises something else entirely:</p> <p>"Across the entire lifetime of this pipeline, every source event is processed exactly once — including under every failure mode."</p> <p>One row can only tell you about state. It cannot tell you about process:</p> <p>Mei answered the question she was asked. We let her answer sign off on a different one.</p> <p>One row fooled the entire team — because it looked exactly like the right answer.</p> <p>I eventually gave this failure mode a name: the Tyranny of the Final State.</p> <p>When the final state looks correct, it quietly steps into every guarantee you never verified, and pretends to be them.</p> <p>The final state is the easiest thing in the system to produce. Upsert absorbs duplicates. Buffers collapse intermediate updates. Idempotent design hides replays. And by the time you query, the system may already have self-healed. You are looking at the world after the repair, not the world at the moment of failure.</p> <p>Six weeks later, during 11.11 peak season, our compliance team in Jakarta pulled the audit trail for a disputed payment. The email subject was short: Duplicate audit record for order 8821 — please explain.</p> <p>Order 8821 shows two audit entries for a single payment event, 0.8 seconds apart. A payment cannot generate two entries. Please explain.</p> <p>Order 8821. The exact row Mei had personally checked.</p> <p>Target table orders: one row, PAID. Fine.</p> <p>Audit table orders_audit — maintained by our own trigger, appended on every write, and not on Mei's seven-item checklist:</p> <p>MySQL binlog: only one UPDATE for 8821 that evening.</p> <p>CDC logs: the event E8821 appeared twice.</p> <p>The room went quiet. I heard Mei breathe in. Ravi slid his notebook across the table — to the line he had written six weeks earlier.</p> <p>"I checked," Mei said, her voice dry. "It was genuinely one row."</p> <p>"It genuinely was one row," I said. "That's the problem."</p> <p>We aligned four timelines — CDC logs, the engine's checkpoint record, PostgreSQL's audit table, and the MySQL binlog — and reconstructed the whole evening:</p> <p>From the first commit at 23:09:45 to the replay at 23:12:42 — less than three minutes.</p> <p>But the fatal window opened earlier. Checkpoint 2847 had completed. Checkpoint 2848 had not yet landed. The interval was 5 seconds, but barriers need to align, state needs to serialize, and the snapshot needs to reach shared storage. The process died just before 2848 committed.</p> <p>So the restore point was still 2847, and the offset was still P0. Everything after P0 — including E8821 — was read again.</p> <p>You delivered the parcel to the customer, then filed the delivery slip. Before you filed it, you got hit by a car. When you woke up, you checked the records, saw no delivery, and delivered it again.</p> <p>The customer received two parcels. But as long as you only ask "does the customer have the parcel?", you will never find out.</p> <p>The crash isn't inside the SQL statement. It's between two commits.</p> <p>A checkpoint isn't magic. It's a bookmark that says "restart here." And between the bookmark and the page, there is a stretch of road nobody owns. That stretch is the entire problem of exactly-once.</p> <p>Turning on checkpointing does not turn a database's ordinary autocommit into a distributed transaction. To make a replay genuinely harmless, three things must still line up after a failure: the source offset, the pending transaction, and the final commit decision.</p> <p>This is not a SeaTunnel problem. Debezium with Kafka Connect, Airbyte, and homegrown CDC all have the same window. The product name changes; the window doesn't.</p> <p>"In this pipeline we need XA," he said. "Otherwise we're gambling."</p> <p>Mei pushed back: "The target has a primary key and we use upsert. Writing twice still leaves one row. XA means tuning max_prepared_transactions, watching pg_prepared_xacts, and re-validating across a failover. That's overkill."</p> <p>Ravi said one line nobody took seriously:</p> <p>"You're not preventing duplicates. You're making them invisible."</p> <p>He wasn't ignoring the cost. Every problem he raised was real:</p> <p>All of that is real operational cost. Ravi never claimed XA was free.</p> <p>His argument reduced to one sentence: if you have promised that transactional side effects will not be duplicated by a replay, upsert cannot pay that bill.</p> <p>For a small regional team, that cost matters twice. We did not have a dedicated DBA in every market, and our auditors in Jakarta were asking for evidence, not architecture diagrams. We chose "good enough." Six weeks later, compliance told us the line we drew was in the wrong place.</p> <p>You can negotiate cost. You cannot guess the boundary. And boundaries get guessed when nobody in the room is willing to say the worst case out loud.</p> <p>"Writing twice still leaves one row" is true — but only on the surface. It is three lies, stacked.</p> <p>True — the target row is one row. But the audit trigger fired twice, and the compliance officer read two entries. Idempotence of a row is not idempotence of a system. You only hid the evidence somewhere outside the row.</p> <p>If the write is UPDATE orders SET version = version + 1 WHERE id = 8821, one replay adds one to version. If it is SET amount = amount + delta, the amount doubles. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE guarantees an atomic statement, not that re-running the statement is harmless.</p> <p>Lie three: an old snapshot overwriting is fine.</p> <p>This is the nastiest one. If the replay brings an older image from an earlier checkpoint, it overwrites the new value with the old one: the order is SHIPPED, and the replay drags it back to PAID. That is state regression, and ordinary upsert has no mechanism to stop it.</p> <p>There is a fourth, quieter layer: sink buffers collapse intermediate updates by key. An order going NEW → PAID → SHIPPED may be collapsed into a single SHIPPED write. The mode was never "one change equals one write" in the first place.</p> <p>Upsert isn't exactly-once. It's a beauty filter for duplicate writes. It hides the evidence; it does not destroy it.</p> <p>I wanted one idea from this incident that people could carry to work.</p> <p>The Tyranny of the Final State: when a system's final state looks correct, it tends to replace every guarantee you never verified, and become the stand-in for "the system is correct."</p> <p>So the Tyranny of the Final State is not a technical problem. It is an incentive problem:</p> <p>We were not fooled by the data. We were fooled by our own verification method — and that method was shaped by "we have to ship today."</p> <p>Mei's seven items were not wrong. The checklist had only one dimension. She verified state; exactly-once promises process. State is a projection of process, and a correct projection does not mean the underlying process was correct.</p> <p>If you remember one line from this article, make it this one:</p> <p>Most teams' "exactly-once" translates to: I checked. Looks right.</p> <p>Better verification does not mean more dashboards. It means deliberately breaking things.</p> <p>We redid that verification in an isolated environment with fixed test keys and a sequence of events we could reconcile. Three drills:</p> <p>Drill 1 — interrupt after the write is issued but before prepare. Does the event replay after recovery, and can a target-side constraint stop it?</p> <p>Drill 2 — interrupt after prepare but before the second-phase commit. Do the in-doubt transactions in pg_prepared_xacts converge — recovered correctly by the coordinator, or left holding locks forever?</p> <p>Drill 3 — target committed, acknowledgement lost, then recover. Does the system mistake "committed" for "failed" and deliver again?</p> <p>The third is the hardest to reproduce reliably. If you cannot do it, write "not verified" — do not pass a random kill -9 off as coverage.</p> <p>Record five things per drill: checkpoint ID, source offset, expected XID, in-doubt transactions on the target, and a timestamp for each stage. After recovery, compare current values key by key, check expected deletes and audit probes, and confirm that in-doubt transactions converged.</p> <p>You cannot prove your brakes work at an intersection with no traffic lights.</p> <p>Mei added one item to the end of her checklist:</p> <p>"If I killed the worker right now, what evidence would prove this row is still correct?"</p> <p>Here is an opinion that may annoy some people.</p> <p>Strict exactly-once is extremely expensive in a distributed system. It needs end-to-end transactional coordination — a transactional sink, an idempotent consumer, a replayable source. And even when all of that is in place, there are still external side effects: the payment callback, the email, the webhook. Those do not roll back with your database transaction.
