They need their own idempotency keys and reconciliation.</p> <p>So my practical advice is: classify by the severity of the side effect, instead of chasing exactly-once everywhere.</p> <p>The lesson of order 8821: we verified it as L0 (final state), but it carried an L1 side effect (an audit trail). Misclassify the level, and the verification is wrong before it starts.</p> <p>This matters more in our region than in most. Across Southeast Asia, data-protection regimes are tightening — Indonesia's PDP Law, Singapore's PDPA, Thailand's PDPA, Vietnam's newer personal-data rules. When an auditor asks for the trail of a single payment, "the table looks right" is not an answer. Duplicate audit entries are not a cosmetic defect; they are a finding with a remediation date attached.</p> <p>Pursuing exactly-once is not wrong. What is wrong is pursuing it indiscriminately, then declaring victory with one row.</p> <p>Order 8821 is still in the target table. PAID, 1299.00.</p> <p>It looks exactly as it did that Friday at 23:17.</p> <p>It never lied to anyone. We asked a question that was easy to answer, then treated the answer as a promise.</p> <p>The line in the deployment log was rewritten. It now says:</p> <p>"End-to-end exactly-once, verified at L1: three failure drills passed, audit-side reconciliation clean."</p> <p>Every extra word in that sentence was bought by two audit entries.</p> <p>So the next time someone tells you they have exactly-once, don't look at their architecture diagram. Don't look at their config. Don't look at their dashboard.</p> <p>DEV Community — A space to discuss and keep up software development and manage your software career</p> <p>Built on Forem — the open source software that powers DEV and other inclusive communities.</p> <p>Made with love and Ruby on Rails. DEV Community © 2016 - 2026.</p> <p>We're a place where coders share, stay up-to-date and grow their careers.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://dev.to/danielnadia/one-row-lied-to-the-whole-team-gbg" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9773"> <h2>#9773. DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/6aeabf9f2efd990530425e58/faP4Su889q_DIgN3wmU9M.png" alt="DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.</p> <p>The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:</p> <p>The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.</p> <p>We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.</p> <p>After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:</p> <p>The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.</p> <p>DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.</p> <p>Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.</p> <p>Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.</p> <p>We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.</p> <p>RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.</p> <p>57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.</p> <p>2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.</p> <p>Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.</p> <p>Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.</p> <p>Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.</p> <p>Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.</p> <p>The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.</p> <p>Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.</p> <p>Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.</p> <p>We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.</p> <p>We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.</p> <p>Adapted from the original RadixArk article.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://huggingface.co/blog/RadixArk/daisyrose-27b-pushing-the-frontier-of-post-trainin" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9772"> <h2>#9772. 162 Blog Posts To Learn About Blockchain Adoption</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://hackernoon.imgix.net/images/github/blockchain-adoption-744.png" alt="162 Blog Posts To Learn About Blockchain Adoption" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Lets geek out. The HackerNoon library is now ranked by reading time created. Start learning by what others read most.</p> <p>Lets geek out. The HackerNoon library is now ranked by reading time created. Start learning by what others read most.</p> <p>Lets geek out. The HackerNoon library is now ranked by reading time created. Start learning by what others read most.</p> <p>Blockchain adoption is the process of integrating and utilizing blockchain technology across various industries and daily life. Increased adoption signifies growing trust in distributed ledger technology and its potential to revolutionize systems.</p> <p>This article provides information on the problems faced by small businesses in emerging countries where banking, other financial technology (fintech) solutions, and identity management are not adopted adequately, and how these problems could be solved using blockchain technology backed by mobile internet usage.</p> <p>Visit the /Learn Repo to find the most read blog posts about any technology.</p> <p>91 Blog Posts To Learn About Blockchain Application</p> <p>Lets geek out. The HackerNoon library is now ranked by reading time created. Start learning by what others read most.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://hackernoon.com/162-blog-posts-to-learn-about-blockchain-adoption?source=rss" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9771"> <h2>#9771. A Routine Docs Lookup Carried the Attack: What ContextCrush (CVE-2026-75130) Teaches About Gating Actions Caused by Tool Output</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=1200,height=627,fit=cover,gravity=auto,format=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fquickchart.io%2Fchart%3Fw%3D1000%26h%3D420%26bkg%3Dwhite%26c%3D%257B%2522type%2522%253A%2522bar%2522%252C%2522data%2522%253A%257B%2522labels%2522%253A%255B%2522Trust%2520every%2520tool%2520result%2522%252C%2522Gate%2520by%2520provenance%2522%255D%252C%2522datasets%2522%253A%255B%257B%2522label%2522%253A%2522Injected%2520high-risk%2520actions%2520that%2520ran%2522%252C%2522data%2522%253A%255B4%252C0%255D%252C%2522backgroundColor%2522%253A%255B%2522%2523d9534f%2522%252C%2522%25232e7d32%2522%255D%257D%255D%257D%252C%2522options%2522%253A%257B%2522title%2522%253A%257B%2522display%2522%253Atrue%252C%2522text%2522%253A%2522Injected%2520high-risk%2520actions%2520that%2520ran%2520%25286-step%2520session%2529%2522%252C%2522fontSize%2522%253A22%257D%252C%2522legend%2522%253A%257B%2522display%2522%253Afalse%257D%257D%257D" alt="A Routine Docs Lookup Carried the Attack: What ContextCrush (CVE-2026-75130) Teaches About Gating Actions Caused by Tool Output" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>The NVD record, published 2026-08-18 on a VulnCheck submission, reads: Context7 through 2.1.2 "contains a prompt injection vulnerability that allows attackers to execute malicious instructions in connected AI coding agents by injecting unsanitized content through the Custom AI Instructions feature served via the MCP server." The listed impacts are credential exfiltration from environment files to an attacker-controlled service and destructive file deletion on the victim's machine, triggered "when the agent makes a routine library documentation request."</p> <p>Context7 provides up-to-date, version-specific documentation to assistants such as Cursor, Claude Code, and Windsurf. It exposes two read-only tools, resolve-library-id and query-docs. Noma's write-up reports about 50,000 GitHub stars and more than 8 million npm downloads, and says it found no evidence of exploitation in the wild.</p> <p>The feature at the center is simple. Library owners can set AI Instructions (also called Custom Rules) in a dashboard to help agents work with their library. Those rules were served through the MCP server to every user who queried that library, with, in Noma's words, no sanitization, content filtering, or distinction from the legitimate documentation.</p> <p>Noma's demonstration used three poisoned rules, each aimed at a different capability of the host agent:</p> <p>Notice that the MCP server itself did none of this. It returned text. The agent, which already held file-read, GitHub, and file-delete tools, did the work. This is the classic confused deputy shape: the attacker has no privileges, the agent has plenty, and the instruction channel and the data channel are the same stream of tokens.</p> <p>The timeline, from Noma's post, is short:</p> <p>The vendor fix, five days after discovery, sanitizes and guards how rules are served and interpreted. The NVD entry was published in August and last modified in October, which is a reminder that CVE records, severity scores, and fix dates can arrive months after the engineering response. Check the primary sources, not a single aggregator.</p> <p>Many approval systems classify tools: reads are free, writes need a prompt. That model assumes the model's next action is independent of what the read returned. It is not. After a read, the model's context contains text an outsider wrote, and the next proposed action may be a function of it.</p> <p>So the unit to gate is not the tool but the action plus its causal history. Two actions with identical arguments deserve different treatment:</p> <p>A gate that only sees the tool name and arguments cannot tell them apart. A gate that records "this action was proposed after untrusted content entered the context" can at least ask a human in the second case.</p> <p>This is a coarse signal and I do not claim it is perfect. Models can launder influence: the user says "follow the library's setup guide," and now every rule is arguably user-sanctioned. That is a policy decision the human should make explicitly, once, with the rule text visible, not implicitly through a docs call.</p> <p>The script below is an illustrative simulation, not a measurement of any real product. It replays a six-step session: one user-driven docs lookup, three injected high-risk actions (credential read, issue creation, delete), one benign user-driven read, and one injected network post.</p> <p>The provenance gate let through exactly the two user-caused actions and stopped all four injected ones. Those four steps become prompts, each showing the human the action and the text that caused it.</p> <p>The hard part in a real system is the cause field. You must compute it, not ask the model. Reasonable approaches:</p> <p>Use this checklist on any agent that connects to third-party MCP servers.</p> <p>Is ContextCrush the same as a vulnerability in the model? No. The model behaved as a language model does when its context says to do something. The flaw was that unsanitized third-party text was delivered in the same channel as trusted documentation, to an agent holding powerful tools.</p> <p>Why do the severity numbers differ so much? The record carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.0 using scope-changed, high-impact metrics, and a CVSS 4.0 score of 6.4. The GitHub advisory labels it medium. Scoring prompt injection is genuinely hard because impact depends on the tools the host agent holds. Use the score for triage order and your own tool inventory for real risk.</p> <p>Would sanitizing the rules fully fix this class? Sanitization helps and the vendor shipped it, but filtering natural language for malicious intent is an arms race. Treat it as one layer. The durable layer is enforcement outside the model: provenance-aware gates, least-privilege tools, and egress control.</p> <p>Does a read-only MCP server need an approval gate at all? The server needs none for its own calls. The agent does need one for the actions that follow its output. Read-only describes the tool's side effects, not the influence of what it returns.</p> <p>Is a human prompt enough? Only if it shows the cause. A prompt that says "delete project/build?" invites a reflexive yes. A prompt that says "delete project/build, proposed after the documentation server returned this text" gives the reviewer what they need to refuse.</p> <p>DEV Community — A space to discuss and keep up software development and manage your software career</p> <p>Built on Forem — the open source software that powers DEV and other inclusive communities.</p> <p>Made with love and Ruby on Rails. DEV Community © 2016 - 2026.</p> <p>We're a place where coders share, stay up-to-date and grow their careers.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://dev.to/ginigenai_hp_0ae441ead91f/a-routine-docs-lookup-carried-the-attack-what-contextcrush-cve-2026-75130-teaches-about-gating-gi4" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9770"> <h2>#9770. Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://huggingface.co/blog/assets/harness-adapters-at-scale/thumbnail.png" alt="Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.</p> <p>Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.</p> <p>Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.</p> <p>Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.</p> <p>We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:</p> <p>Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.</p> <p>For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.</p> <p>RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.</p> <p>This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.</p> <p>Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:</p> <p>We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.</p> <p>A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:</p> <p>Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:</p> <p>858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.</p> <p>A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.</p> <p>Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.</p> <p>Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.</p> <p>This example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.</p> <p>The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.</p> <p>Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:</p> <p>The figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.</p> <p>harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.</p> <p>We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.</p> <p>For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.</p> <p>To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.</p> <p>The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best).</p> <p>We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.</p> <p>Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).</p> <p>As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.</p> <p>The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:</p> <p>Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.</p> <p>We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.</p> <p>The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.</p> <p>Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?</p> <p>We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.</p> <p>We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:</p> <p>The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.</p> <p>Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):</p> <p>"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.</p> <p>With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).</p> <p>Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.</p> <p>Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.</p> <p>The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.</p> <p>The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.</p> <p>This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.</p> <p>Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.</p> <p>During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.</p> <p>On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.</p> <p>This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.</p> <p>We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.</p> <p>Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.</p> <p>For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.</p> <p>For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.</p> <p>All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).</p> <p>The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.</p> <p>To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.</p> <p>Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.</p> <p>What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?</p> <p>We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?</p> <p>Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.</p> <p>We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.</p> <p>This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.</p> <p>This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.</p> <p>Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.</p> <p>However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.</p> <p>Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.</p> <p>In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.</p> <p>We also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.</p> <p>Train open models with RL inside real agent harnesses</p> <p>Explore async reinforcement learning with AsyncGRPOTrainer</p> <p>Thanks for such a nice and detailed blog on it. Can you also share, how many iterations did this take, and roughly how long end to end? What would be the minimum GPU requirements to train. Also curious how you think the adapter holds up when the harness changes.</p> <p>Nice article guys!For adapters merging, one cool idea would be to do MOPD where the student is Qwen3.8-27B (the original one) and teachers are the RL lora adapted one. The random selection of the harness selects the teacher.</p> <p>Train open models with RL inside real agent harnesses</p> <p>Explore async reinforcement learning with AsyncGRPOTrainer</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://huggingface.co/blog/harness-adapters-at-scale" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9769"> <h2>#9769. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p><h2 style="text-align: left;"><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEjF7I9iAp1Tfc6kFmKNOYqqI2V1NjZ1ltfemNKGCo1nvQlCy0DWGe_hNag4uruW_SW6tMwc0M8sa4O7ca4zQ6Hiiu6TDi4VAohA3aTPmU4KuRqBC2KQpg3PB_55tjbwwO9ko2xAW-9QQdfpph0xVKiCDiMRKkrL8clOk90wa1arfXGW0VKIO182Qb31vw=s1920" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="Grammarly vs prowritingaid" border="0" height="360" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEjF7I9iAp1Tfc6kFmKNOYqqI2V1NjZ1ltfemNKGCo1nvQlCy0DWGe_hNag4uruW_SW6tMwc0M8sa4O7ca4zQ6Hiiu6TDi4VAohA3aTPmU4KuRqBC2KQpg3PB_55tjbwwO9ko2xAW-9QQdfpph0xVKiCDiMRKkrL8clOk90wa1arfXGW0VKIO182Qb31vw=w640-h360" title="Grammarly vs prowritingaid" width="640" /></a></div></h2><div style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b><span><a name="more"></a></span>ProWritingAid VS Grammarly:<span style="color: #3c4043;"><span style="background-color: white; font-size: 14px;"> </span></span></b></span><span style="color: #3c4043; font-family: Comfortaa;"><span style="font-size: 14px;"> When it comes to English grammar, there are two Big Players that everyone knows of: the Grammarly and ProWritingAid. but you are wondering which one to choose so here we write a detail article which will help you to choose the best one for you so Let's start</span></span></div><h2 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">What is Grammarly?</span></h2><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><br /></span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Features of Grammarly</b></span></h3><p></p><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Spelling and Word Suggestion:</b> Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Create a Personal Dictionary:</b> The Grammarly app allows you to add words to your personal dictionary so that the same mistake isn't highlighted every time you run Grammarly.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Different English Style</b>: Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Plagiarism:</b> This feature helps you detect if a text has been plagiarized by comparing it with over eight billion web pages.</span></li> <li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Wordiness:</b> This tool will help you check your writing for long and hard-to-read sentences. It also shows you how to shorten sentences so that they are more concise.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Passive Voice:</b> The program also notifies users when passive voice is used too frequently in a document.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Punctuations:</b> This feature flags all incorrect and missing punctuation.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Repetition:</b> The tool provides recommendations for replacing the repeated word.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Proposition:</b> Grammarly identifies misplaced and confused prepositions.</span><center><br /></center> <div id="atContainer-8a426783aef805554f3d96c19f8beeb7"></div> </li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Plugins:</b> It offers Microsoft Word, Microsoft Outlook, and Google Chrome plugins.</span></li></ul><p></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><br /></span></p><h2 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">What is ProWritingAid?</span></h2><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing. </span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Features of ProWriting Aid</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:</span></p><p></p><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Grammar checker and spell checker:</b> This tool helps you to find all grammatical and spelling errors.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Find repeated words:</b>  The tool also allows you to search for repeated words and phrases in your content.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Context-sensitive style suggestions:</b>  You can find the exact style of writing you intend and suggest if it flows well in your writing.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Check the readability of your content:</b> Pro Writing Aid helps you identify the strengths and weaknesses of your article by pointing out difficult sentences and paragraphs.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Sentence Length: </b>It also indicates the length of your sentences.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Check Grammatical error:</b> It also checks your work for any grammatical errors or typos, as well.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Overused words:</b> As a writer, you might find yourself using the same word repeatedly. ProWritingAid's overused words checker helps you avoid this lazy writing mistake.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Consistency:</b> Check your work for inconsistent usage of open and closed quotation marks.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Echoes:</b> Check your writing for uniformly repetitive words and phrases.</span></li></ul><p></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Difference between Grammarly and Pro-Writing Aid</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Grammarly</b> and <b>ProWritingAid</b> are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Grammarly vs ProWritingAid</span></h3><p></p><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Grammarly </b>is a writing enhancement tool that offers suggestions for grammar, vocabulary, and syntax whereas <b>ProWritingAid</b> offers world-class grammar and style checking, as well as advanced reports to help you strengthen your writing.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Grammarly</b> provides Android and IOS apps whereas <b>ProWritingAid</b> doesn't have a mobile or IOS app.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Grammarly</b> offers important suggestions about mistakes you've made whereas <b>ProWritingAid</b>  shows more suggestions than Grammarly but all recommendations are not accurate</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Grammarly</b> has a more friendly UI/UX whereas the ProWritingAid interface is not friendly as Grammarly.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Grammarly</b> is an accurate grammar checker for non-fiction writing whereas <b>ProWritingAid</b> is an accurate grammar checker for fiction writers.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Grammarly</b> finds grammar and punctuation mistakes, whereas <b>ProWritingAid</b> identifies run-on sentences and fragments.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Grammarly</b> provides 24/7 support via submitting a ticket and sending emails. <b>ProWritingAid’s</b> support team is available via email, though the response time is approximately 48 hours.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Grammarly</b> offers many features in its free plan, whereas<b> ProWritingAid</b> offers some basic features in the free plan.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Grammarly </b>does not offer much feedback on big picture writing; <b>ProWritingAid</b> offers complete feedback on big picture writing.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><b>Grammarly</b> is a better option for accuracy, whereas <b>ProWritingAid</b> is better for handling fragmented sentences and dialogue. It can be quite useful for fiction writers.</span></li></ul><p></p><h2 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Pricing Difference</span></h2><p></p><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">ProWritingAid comes with three pricing structures. The full-year cost of ProWritingAid is $79, while its lifetime plans cost $339. You also can opt for a monthly plan of $20.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Grammarly offers a Premium subscription for $30/month for a monthly plan  $20/month for quarterly and $12/month for an annual subscription.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">The Business plan costs $12.50 per month for each member of your company.</span></li></ul><p></p><h2 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">ProWritingAid vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons</span></h2><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Grammarly Pros</span></h3><p></p><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">It allows you to fix common mistakes like grammar and spelling.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Offers most features in the free plan</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Allows you to edit a document without affecting the formatting.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Active and passive voice checker</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Personal dictionary </span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Plagiarism checker (paid version)</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Proofread your writing and correct all punctuation, grammar, and spelling errors.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Allows you to make changes to a document without altering its formatting.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Helps users improve vocabulary</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">User-friendly interface</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Browser extensions and MS word add-ons</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Available on all major devices and platforms</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Grammarly will also offer suggestions to improve your style.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Enhance the readability of your sentence</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Free mobile apps </span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Offers  free version</span></li></ul><p></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Grammarly Cons</span></h3><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Supports only English </span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Customer support only via email</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Limits to 150,000 words</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Subscription plans can be a bit pricey </span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Plagiarism checker is only available in a premium plan</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Doesn’t offer a free trial</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">No refund policy</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">The free version is ideal for basic spelling and grammatical mistakes, but it does not correct advanced writing issues.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Some features are not available for Mac.</span></li></ul><p></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">ProwritingAid Pros</span></h3><p></p><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">It offers more than 20 different reports to help you improve your writing.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Less expensive than other grammar checkers.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">This tool helps you strengthen your writing style as it offers big-picture feedback.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">ProWritingAid has a life plan with no further payments required.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Compatible with Google Docs!</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Prowritingaid works on both Windows and Mac.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">They offer more integrations than most tools.</span></li></ul><p></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">ProWritingAid Cons</span></h3><p></p><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Editing can be a little more time-consuming when you add larger passages of text.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">ProWritingAid currently offers no mobile app for Android or iOS devices.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Plagiarism checker is only available in premium plans.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">All recommendations are not accurate</span></li></ul><p></p><h2 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Summarizing the Ginger VS Grammarly: My Recommendation</span></h2><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.</span></p><p></p><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">For example, go for Grammarly  if you are a non-fiction writer</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Go for ProWritingAid if you are a fiction writer.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">ProWritingAid is better at catching errors found in long-form content. However, Grammarly is more suited to short blog posts and other similar tasks.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">ProWritingAid helps you clean up your writing by checking for style, structure, and content while Grammarly focuses on grammar and punctuation.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.</span></li></ul><p></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.</span></p><p><br /></p><p><br /></p></p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://techncruncher.blogspot.com/2022/03/prowritingaid-vs-grammarly-which.html" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9768"> <h2>#9768. AzuraCast's 2 App Matches and 14,742 Title Matches Describe Two Different Surfaces</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=1200,height=627,fit=cover,gravity=auto,format=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F91tvw5o9syhcsxl55vre.png" alt="AzuraCast's 2 App Matches and 14,742 Title Matches Describe Two Different Surfaces" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>AzuraCast combines a web radio control panel, public player pages, station roles, and an API. A single title search can surface both the operational console and the listener-facing side. Treating those matches as one asset population hides the credential boundary.</p> <p>ZoomEye SDK probes on 22 November 2026 used sub_type=all, page 1, and pagesize=1. The exact query app="AzuraCast" returned 2 matches. title="AzuraCast" returned 14,742. The queries completed between 06:46 and 06:47 Asia/Shanghai.</p> <p>The large difference is not evidence that 14,740 installations lack the application fingerprint. It means the two index fields describe different evidence. A title can be attached to a public station site, a login page, an API error page, or a reverse-proxy page. The app value is narrower and may be absent from many deployments.</p> <p>AzuraCast supports role-based user management with global and per-station permissions. Each installation also exposes API documentation, and operators can create API keys from the web interface. A public player page may be harmless while the adjacent administration path can change playlists, mounts, users, or station configuration.</p> <p>The project's changelog warns that allowing users to edit raw Liquidsoap configuration has security implications in multi-tenant environments because the scripting language can call external processes and read system files. That setting turns a station-level role into a much stronger authority over the host. An inventory that records only "AzuraCast exposed" misses this distinction.</p> <p>For each owned installation, record the web base path, API path, public player routes, admin routes, reverse-proxy rules, and TLS certificate. Confirm whether the API is reachable from the internet and which roles can create or use keys.</p> <p>Expose public players deliberately. Put administration behind a VPN, access proxy, or tightly scoped network rule. Review global and per-station roles, remove unused API keys, and disable raw Liquidsoap editing unless a trusted administrator has a documented need. Keep station credentials out of public page source and client-side configuration.</p> <p>Use the project's API documentation to enumerate active keys and permissions. A valid login does not establish least privilege. Rotate keys tied to former staff or decommissioned stations.</p> <p>The 2 application matches are a narrow product signal. The 14,742 title matches are a broad web clue. Neither number proves vulnerability. Together they show why identity, route, and permission review must follow the measurement.</p> <p>DEV Community — A space to discuss and keep up software development and manage your software career</p> <p>Built on Forem — the open source software that powers DEV and other inclusive communities.</p> <p>Made with love and Ruby on Rails. DEV Community © 2016 - 2026.</p> <p>We're a place where coders share, stay up-to-date and grow their careers.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://dev.to/kozhevniko/azuracasts-2-app-matches-and-14742-title-matches-describe-two-different-surfaces-3add" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9767"> <h2>#9767. Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://huggingface.co/blog/assets/inkling2mini/thumbnail.png" alt="Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.</p> <p>Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!</p> <p>We ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.</p> <p>This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.</p> <p>Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.</p> <p>Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.</p> <p>Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.</p> <p>Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.</p> <p>In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.</p> <p>Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.</p> <p>Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.</p> <p>In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.</p> <p>We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.</p> <p>You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.</p> <p>To set the number of loops in the research checkpoint, you can modify the loop_num_passes in text_config as follows. The example below uses two loops.</p> <p>For an image prompt, replace messages in either example with the list below and infer as usual.</p> <p>Pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).</p> <p>Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.</p> <p>In this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.</p> <p>If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.</p> <p>Llama App lets you easily run and manage local language models on macOS (from the menu bar) or Windows (system tray). It’s built on llama.cpp, and by the same team. The app also provides a local OpenAI-compatible API for easy integration with coding agents, editors, and scripts.</p> <p>For the Inkling 2 Mini release we provide GGUF 4-bit (IQ4_NL) and 8-bit (Q8_0) quants for both models.</p> <p>If you’re on Linux or you want to serve the model from the CLI, you can run the following command for the fixed-loop model:</p> <p>To run the variable-loop model, you can run</p> <p>To load the 8-bit weights, change the suffix to :Q8_0.</p> <p>Here we ask the 4-bit model to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists. Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic.</p> <p>Inkling 2 Mini comes with Day 0 support inside SGLang. You can install the latest version of SGLang and execute the following to get the server up and running. One prerequisite to take care of is to run it on SM103.</p> <p>After the server is up you should be able to request the APIs like so</p> <p>One can also enable multimodality by setting --enable-multimodal.</p> <p>SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.</p> <p>We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.</p> <p>We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.</p> <p>MLX inference works with the original checkpoint too. In this case, the native nvfp4 + mxfp8 quantization scheme is used without reconversion: you get the original quality the authors intended.</p> <p>We have given Inkling 2 Mini a shot in many fun tasks, check them out in this section.</p> <p>The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.</p> <p>Build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.</p> <p>Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889)</p> <p>We gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. The shader draws the scene from code without loading the reference image or any other assets. It uses time to animate the swirling sky, the glow of the stars, the swaying cypress, and the flicker of the village windows.</p> <p>Inkling rendered and reviewed its work over 24 rounds of screenshot checks. We recorded the final animation frame by frame at 1080p and 60 fps on an Apple M4 Max.</p> <p>In this folder, starry-night.jpg is Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889, public domain). Recreate it as a living painting: a single self-contained index.html (all code inline, no external files, libraries or network requests) that fills the browser window and runs smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Everything must be generated procedurally in code, for example with WebGL shaders; the page must not load, embed or sample starry-night.jpg or any other image. Stay faithful to the painting's composition and palette (the great spiral and swirling currents of the sky, the haloed stars, the glowing crescent moon, the dark flame-like cypress on the left, the rolling hills, and the village with its church spire), rendered in Van Gogh's thick, directional brushstrokes, and bring it to life: the sky's swirls flow, the stars and moon pulse with light, the cypress sways, and the village windows glow and flicker. Aim for the most impressive result you can make. A helper is provided: run node shot.js --help to see how to screenshot index.html at several moments; look at the screenshots next to the reference and keep improving until you are satisfied, then reply with a short summary of what you made.</p> <p>We gave Inkling 2 Mini a photo of a hand-drawn Trip Split wireframe and a one-paragraph prompt in the Pi coding harness. Inkling used the sketch’s labels, sample expenses, and handwritten notes to build the expense list, add-expense form, and balances view in a single HTML file with vanilla CSS and JavaScript.
